title: Snap States, Trimmed Gutters, Shape ASCII, Glass & attr()
description: Scroll-state container queries, margin-trim gutters, a shape-aware ASCII renderer, refracting glass lenses, and typed attr() components.

drops.title: Snap State Choreography
drops.description: A snap rail, a sticky header and a fading scroll box animated entirely by @container scroll-state() — no scroll listeners.
drops.concept: container-type: scroll-state lets an element ask the scroller about its own position, and plain @container rules react. This drop wires all three states at once: snapped: x scales the settled card in a snap rail, stuck: top thickens a sticky header, and scrollable: top/bottom fades the edges of an overflow box. Because the state resolves in style, the transition starts on the same frame the scroller commits — and a shim button shows what the same CSS looks like when JS has to mirror the states instead.
drops.source: Una Kravets & Adam Argyle — 'CSS scroll-state queries' on Chrome for Developers

interaction.mouse: Scroll or drag the snap rail; scroll the sticky-header panel and the fading overflow box.
interaction.click: Advance the rail, force the JS shim, and retune the settle duration.
interaction.touch: All three regions are touch-scrollable; the panel stacks under the demos on narrow screens.

drops.title: Trimmed Gutters
drops.description: Children keep their own margins; margin-trim drops only the ones touching the container's edges, in three different layouts.
drops.concept: A component that carries its own margin is easy to reuse and annoying to contain — which is why design systems grow a thicket of :first-child and :last-child resets. margin-trim moves the decision to the container: it discards exactly the child margins adjoining its edges, in logical axes. The drop toggles none / block / inline / block-inline live across a card stack, a horizontal chip rail and a prose column, with an overlay that highlights the space being reclaimed.
drops.source: Dave Cross — 'margin-trim' on Modern CSS Daily

interaction.mouse: Scroll each of the three boxes to see the trimmed edge behave under overflow.
interaction.click: Switch trim mode, change the child margin, and toggle the overlay showing what gets removed.
interaction.touch: Buttons and slider are full-width on mobile; all three demos scroll by touch.

drops.title: Shape-Aware ASCII
drops.description: Six probes per cell build a shape vector, then the renderer searches every glyph for the nearest ink distribution.
drops.concept: A luminance ramp only knows how bright a cell is, so edges turn to mush. This renderer rasterises all 67 candidate glyphs once, reduces each to a six-value shape vector at asymmetric probe points, normalises per probe so heavy glyphs cannot dominate, then finds the nearest match for every cell of the source. A neighbour-contrast pass pushes each cell away from its surroundings so diagonals resolve into slashes. Three live surfaces — a rotating solid, editable type and a lit sphere — plus a toggle that drops back to a plain ramp for comparison.
drops.source: Edoardo Lunardi — 'Beyond the Luminance Ramp: A Shape-Aware ASCII Renderer' on Codrops

interaction.mouse: Slide cell size, contrast and neighbour strength and watch the vocabulary shift live.
interaction.click: Toggle the luminance-ramp comparison, pause the animation, or type a new word for surface b.
interaction.touch: Panel stacks below the surfaces; all controls are touch-sized.

drops.title: Glass Lens
drops.description: Three draggable lenses push a generated normal map through feDisplacementMap inside backdrop-filter.
drops.concept: Blur alone reads as frosted plastic; real glass bends what is behind it. Each lens generates a convex normal map on a canvas — flat in the centre, steep at the rim — hands it to an SVG feImage, and uses it as the displacement map for the backdrop. Radius, refraction scale, bevel falloff and blur are all live, the lenses drag and can be set drifting, and a badge reports whether the engine accepts url() inside backdrop-filter or is falling back to blur plus the specular shell.
drops.source: archisvaze/liquid-glass — an interactive iOS-26-style liquid glass effect for the web

interaction.mouse: Drag any of the three lenses across the plate and watch the type bend under the rim.
interaction.click: Set the lenses drifting, or retune radius, refraction, bevel and blur.
interaction.touch: Pointer Events handle touch dragging directly; the plate disables touch scrolling while dragging.

drops.title: Attribute-Driven Components
drops.description: Meters, ratings, a gauge, an avatar stack and a badge — configured only by HTML attributes, via typed attr().
drops.concept: Typed attr() lets CSS read a number, a percentage or an angle straight out of the markup, so a component can be configured the way HTML was always meant to configure things: with attributes. None of the five components here carries an inline style or a custom property in its markup — the stylesheet reads data-value, data-stars, data-angle, data-i and data-count directly, and the controls only ever call setAttribute. Engines without typed attr() get a six-line mirror shim so the same CSS still resolves.
drops.source: MDN Web Docs — CSS attr(); typed attr() shipped in Firefox 155 (Sept 2026)

interaction.mouse: Drag the four sliders — each one only rewrites an HTML attribute.
interaction.click: Randomise every component at once; hover an avatar to lift it out of the stack.
interaction.touch: Cards reflow to a single column and the panel stacks above them.
